content: #Project announcements > FloatLib: Verified Floating-Point Arithmetic in lean @ 💬

Hi Robert, neat paper.

I'm wondering if you can clarify the difference between FloatLib and FloatSpec by Beneficial AI Foundation? Your paper mentions it in passing,

In Lean, FloatSpec develops Flocq-style theory and IEEE models, while FLoPS formalizes P3109 semantics and rounding, with executable arithmetic and refinement proofs. FloatLib combines extensible numerical representations with cost-based selection among certified software implementations.

To me, this explanation (and Table 1) doesn't exactly give a complete comparison of your two implementations, nor fully justifies why a practitioner should choose to use one library over another.

I'm also a bit surprised that you neglected to mention Float.Model which was added Lean 4.33. In particular, it may be worth citing @Julia Markus Himmel's excellent blog post where they suggest downstream Float implementations should:

  • Prove that the Float.Model type is equivalent to your type corresponding to the IEEE binary64 format without NaN payloads, and that all of the operations commute with that equivalence
  • Transfer lemmas about your nice downstream float type to Float.Model along that equivalence

Jeremy Tan said:

Do you have unums/posits formalised?

Hi Jeremy! Yes, we have posits following the 2022 standard, parameterized by arbitrary width not just posit8/16/32. This includes executable arithmetic, proofs of the standard’s rounding rules, and exact quire accumulation within its capacity bound. We don’t currently implement the other unum families but if needed we can! I feel like posits are the best way: ) we also did contact John Gustafson (who created posits) before working on this! His ideas were very cool and in some of our experiments we found them to be extremely accurate, which is why we focussed on the speed. As of now floatlib matches stillwater universal (default posit library) in speed and fully verified!

Hi Jack, thanks for reading it carefully! That’s fair: the paragraph and table should explain the practical differences more clearly and i will expand the site and the future paper more in depth for this:)!

Let me first start of by saying that the BFAI has done a great job with FloatSpec but personally to me I found some limitations with it. For first, both libraries draw on Flocq, and there is substantial overlap in their mathematical foundations. FloatSpec follows Flocq’s organization closely, with generic radix/exponent formats, rounding theory, error bounds, and IEEE models. If you’re bringing over an argument expressed using Flocq’s definitions and lemmas, that correspondence is useful.

However again to emphasize, we put considerable effort on running the arithmetic efficiently while proving the implementations correct. We ensured to also make the API cleaner to use and easy to support all numerical types like IEEE binary and decimal, arbitrary- width posits, P3109, and custom formats and rounding rules. For the speed: we have tables, machine-word kernels, and wider limb algorithms that sit behind a shared interface, with each certified backend proved equal to its encoded specification. Separate theorems connect those results to real rounding, error bounds, and exactness.

I took a closer look at FloatSpec revision 158263e. Its rounded IEEE operations are marked noncomputable, but the underlying integer algorithms can be compiled through wrappers. We did this and proved in Lean that the wrappers equal the original operations. The plot below compares those compiled operations with FloatLib, using matching inputs, formats, and nearest-even rounding. These are preliminary results from one timing round. Addition and subtraction completed at 8, 16, and 24 significand bits. After removing the time limits, higher-precision runs hit stack or memory limit as it recursively assigns values! I traced the bottleneck to binaryPositiveOfNatSucc, which constructs the mantissa’s Positive representation one increment at a time. That conversion dominates addition and subtraction; their large ratios reflect this particular implementation bottleneck. Multiplication, division, and square root follow different paths and completed through 4,096 significand bits. All completed numerical checks agreed with our exact-arithmetic oracle.

On Float.Model, we do discuss the connection in §3.6, “Parsing and Lean’s native types,” including a Lean example transferring native addition into FloatLib arithmetic (we had done this actually a month ago in TorchLean for FP32). But I will also add Julia’s blog to the list!

One thing to keep in mind is that our representation conversions account for the fact that FloatLib retains NaN details that Lean’s model canonicalizes. We have binary32/64 addition and subtraction bridges for finite inputs, allowing overflow in the result, and square-root commutation covering all inputs after that canonicalization. Multiplication and division bridges currently have additional conditions. We haven’t completed an unrestricted “all operations commute” result. Thanks for pointing this out and I will expand more on the related work!
